speakeroldname: Hon. W. Bennett Campbell (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the welcome duty of reminding Hon. Members that tomorrow is Remembrance Day. Services of commemoration will be held across our country as Canadians pause to reflect on the sacrifices that were made in their name. Also, as is traditional, a few days ago Canada held a service of commemoration at the Vimy Memorial in France. On that occasion the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) paid tribute, on behalf of all Canadians, to those soldiers who, 65 years ago, won everlasting glory at Vimy Ridge.
On Remembrance Day itself, thousands of Canadians will gather around the National War Memorial in our capital. This memorial has stood as a symbol of our nation's homage for over 40 years. This year, for the first time, the War Memorial bears the inscriptions 1939-45 and 1950-53, reflecting the ceremony last summer when the memorial was officially rededicated to include those who served in the Second World War and Korea.
However, the inscription I will best remember this year was the one I read during our pilgrimage to Dieppe, France, last August, to mark the fortieth anniversary of that costly raid. 1 had the privilege to be in the company of many of the 5,000 Canadians who landed on those Dieppe beaches in 1942, as well as distinguished representatives of the House of Commons, the Senate and veterans' organizations from across Canada. Together we attended a service at Puys where, as Hon. Members are aware, the Royal Regiment was decimated 40 years before.
A plaque on the Puys Memorial contains words that reveal the true meaning of Remembrance Day; they could be used to describe all the 100,000 Canadians who died in World War I, World War II and Korea. The plaque reads:
You who are alive on this beach, remember that these men died far from home that others, here and everywhere, might freely enjoy life in God's mercy.
Hear, hear!

Madam
Speaker, yesterday the Government and the Official Opposition agreed to adjourn the House of Commons after Remembrance Day eulogies, as a special tribute to our fallen comrades. I am very disappointed that the New Democratic Party refused to participate in that gesture to honour those who
made the ultimate sacrifice for their country. It would have been an additional recognition on behalf of Canada's veterans.
On behalf of the Progressive Party of Canada I am proud to offer our feelings on this Remembrance Day. We join in the resounding praise of the dedication, bravery and courage which Canadian veterans gave our country. Through the many conflicts in which we, as a country, have been involved, our veterans have offered the ultimate sacrifice for freedom, their lives.
For that sacrifice we owe our veterans more than our thoughts just once a year. We owe them the security and freedom of life that they fought for and won. We owe them the day-to-day confidence which comes from knowing that, if they need it, aging, disabled veterans can count on Canada the way we counted on them. To this end, Canadians in general are very supportive of any Government action directed at guaranteeing veterans a respectable standard of living.
Much has been done through the combined efforts of veterans' organizations such as the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans, the Royal Canadian Legion, the War Amputations of Canada, the United Veterans' Organization, and the federal Government. We must also strive to guarantee that our aging disabled veterans can look forward to even better service in the future. To this end we must be united in our efforts to act expeditiously in all matters pertaining to veterans, including their benefits, general well-being, and related services. We should use any and every means at our disposal to fulfil these responsibilities.
Members of Parliament will be travelling to their homes to join in the ceremonies at eleven o'clock on November 11. These ceremonies in local villages, towns and cities will, for a brief period, join us all in a spirit of remorse, yet pride, in the brotherhood of spirits and mind, but, most important, will join us in the renewed belief that any war cannot be tolerated, that we cannot afford the cost to life that today's wars inflict.
For the 740,000 Canadian veterans in Canada, we must all combine to pay tribute to their past and pay careful attention to their future. For those no longer with us, we can only be thankful for their contribution, and we will remember them always.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, we wish to thank you again for giving us the opportunity to have this occasion when we can speak of those who served this country in many ways over many years.

November 10, 1982
Remembrance Day
We think in particular of those who lost their lives in World War 1 and World War II, and in the Korean War. We are also conscious of others through the years who have lost their lives because of what has happened to them following their service. We pay them tribute for what they have done. We give them our thanks. We welcome the opportunity every time the month of November comes around to pay our tribute to them. We also express our thanks to those who have worked for us in the years gone by; we thank them for what they have done to increase the provisions of the legislation which we have now, helping to build a country which will carry on in this way.
We are also conscious of the fact, Madam Speaker, there are some veterans still alive today who, for many years, will be expressing their tribute in one way or another. Today we give them a special word of praise, and we thank the Minister for making this opportunity possible.
At the same time, there are some of us who are deeply concerned about what is ahead on the question of wars, not only for this part of the world but for all the world. We hope one of these days we can find some other way to solve some of the problems so that our nations are not completely torn apart. We are grateful for the efforts of the people of this country, and of various Governments, who are concerned about world affairs. It is indeed a very important effort. Many centuries ago some people declared that their swords should be turned into ploughshares. That is our view, also. Our main concern is to build a world of peace for all those who are in it.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, I would like to join the previous speakers in saying a few words about Remembrance Day, a time for commemorating the sacrifices made by our soldiers in the two World Wars and the Korean War, in the name of democracy. As Chairman of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, I wish to pay a special tribute to those who served with me during the war from 1939 to 1945 and who lie buried in European soil. They volunteered their services and gave their lives for their country and for democracy. Madam Speaker, we must realize the price these young men and women paid so that future generations would be able to enjoy the kind of life and the democratic system of government we have today, and we should stop and think about the tremendous sacrifice these soldiers made so generously. Once again, Madam Speaker, I wish to join the previous speakers in paying tribute to these men and women.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY EFFECT OF FUEL TAX AND INCREASED TOLLS
ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY EFFECT OF FUEL TAX AND INCREASED TOLLS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have seen the disastrous results of federal greed in the oil and gas industry and now we see it with respect to the St. Lawrence Seaway. Thanks to ever rising Seaway tolls, a discriminatory transportation fuel tax, and the absence, still, of a coherent shipping policy, the Seaway is expected to post an $8 million deficit this year. Canadian shippers are in a neck-and-neck race with foreign shippers and other transportation modes to gain shipping contracts, and at every turn they are being tripped up by the federal Government. I therefore move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis):
That the federal Government remove the discriminatory transportation fuel compensation recovery charge, reduce the 1983 toll increase to 6 per cent in keeping with the six and five formula, and initiate a shipping policy without further delay, before the St. Lawrence Seaway system joins the ranks of Maislin, Massey-Ferguson and Dome Petroleum.

subsubtopic: "BLACK BOOK" USED BY CROWN COUNSEL-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice, but first I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate him publicly on his appointment to the portfolio. Also I would like to ask him some questions concerning where he stands on important and fundamental issues in the country.
The Minister will know that the Government has spent, or will be spending, at least $35 million in connection with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in Canada, attempting to publicize the advantages to Canadian people of the new Charter. Yet, legislatively and in the area of policy initiatives, the Government has in many instances been diametrically opposed to the spirit and letter of the Charter of Rights. One example is the question of the "black book" which has been bank-rolled by the Government. There has been participation by the Department of Justice in the preparation of the black book to be distributed to Crown counsel across the country, in which they are instructed on how to circumvent the operation of the Charter of Rights.
Now that the Minister of Justice has had a chance to consider his position in his new portfolio, does he sanction the use of these black books across the country, or will he prohibit their use by Crown counsel on the federal side? I would at least like him to indicate whether or not he is prepared, in the spirit of freedom of information to which the Government is apparently committed, to make these black books public so that the people of Canada and parliamentarians could see precisely what instructions are given to Crown counsel.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: "BLACK BOOK" USED BY CROWN COUNSEL-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 thank the Hon. Member for his congratulations. 1 would like to tell him that the so-called black book is not a federal book at all. We began to work with provincial Attorneys General to try to work out such a common book of instruction to counsel. We found that we were not able to agree with many of the provinces on their interpretation of the Charter. Therefore, the joint project was separated into two projects-the provincial black book and the federal "white book". We have a separate set of instructions to federal prosecutors. I will certainly consider whether or not it would be appropriate to make it public. I have some doubts about that since I think the important part of the work of federal prosecutors in the courts involves a lot of discretion. I am not sure that we would want to indicate in a litigation circumstance of an adversary nature the exact tenor of the instructions they had received, which might put the federal counsel in prejudice.

November 10, 1982
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, the point I am making to the Minister is that there was more than a hint of hypocrisy in the Government's position with respect to the Charter of Rights and the rights of every individual in this country.
By way of preface to my supplementary question, I want to point out to him that, with the exception of language rights, there has not been any instance where the federal Department of Justice has intervened in the courts in support of either the Diefenbaker Bill of Rights or with respect to the new Charter of Rights. I think it is a shame that the Government is not promoting the rights of individual citizens.
Will the Minister tell the House whether or not he is now prepared, as a matter of directive and policy in his department, to consider supporting the Charter of Rights position before the courts? Also, will the Minister at least consider the suggestion that an independent institute be established to which litigants, who have worth-while cases involving constitutional matters in support of Charter of Rights matters, would be able to apply and receive either assistance by way of counsel or monetary assistance for their own counsel before the appeal courts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member knows that in cases of this kind decisions are made on a case by case basis as to what position federal counsel should take. Very frequently there are cases where we decide not to challenge a decision of a lower court, not to intervene in any way, and those are obviously situations in which we are satisfied with the decision as it was reached, or at least are not sufficiently dissatisfied so as to take the opposite side.
1 cannot honestly tell the Hon. Member whether there is any case in which we have appeared to support a litigant or not. There is such a diversity of cases. I will try to find out whether or not that is the case. But that really is not a test.
Nevertheless, in addition to what we are doing in court, Madam Speaker, we have a vast project under way involving the scrutiny of 23 volumes of federal statutes and 16,000 pages of the 1978 count of the consolidated regulations, to attempt to see in advance as far as we can, without pre-empting the decisions of the courts, clear cases of conflict between the new Bill of Rights and the Statutes or Regulations of Canada.
Madam Speaker, the only consequence of that action is that it will at least be a make-work project for lawyers.

Madam Speaker, I have a final supplementary for the Minister of Justice. As he will know, his colleague, the Solicitor General, has been going up and down the country over the past couple of years supporting a proposition for the removal of the moratorium on the use of writs of assistance. These writs are clear intrusions into the
privacy of Canadian citizens, giving unlimited right to the police of this country to break and enter into the homes of Canadians. That is clearly against the charter, the principle of unreasonable search. Has the Minister considered his position with respect to writs of assistance, and has the Minister of Justice told the Solicitor General to refrain from promoting this idea which is contrary to the Charter of Rights?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we certainly have a dialogue in our Government with the public on what the state of the law should be. I can tell the Hon. Member that there have been no new writs of assistance issued since 1976,1 think, and the ones that exist are used now only in the enforcement of the Narcotic Control Act and the Food and Drugs Act, and 1 understand only where reasonable cause exists on the part of an officer to believe that the premises actually contain some drugs. The matter is under further examination, but we have certainly eliminated the worst abuses in the law as it stands. We will be considering this further over the months. If the Hon. Member has any submissions to make to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, we will certainly be very pleased to have a dialogue with him on those.

subsubtopic: ACTIVITIES OF FORMER ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE CORPORAL
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General. It relates to a matter on which he has now been briefed concerning the security incident, apparently code named "Long Knife", details of which have been widely published in the past few days. Because this former corporal of the RCMP security service appeared in disguise last night on a national television program and virtually confessed to having sold out a double agent in Montreal to an agent of the Soviet KGB for payment of S3,500, will the Minister give an explanation of why this man was never charged but is able now to continue to profit from his apparently traitorous activities?

subsubtopic: ACTIVITIES OF FORMER ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE CORPORAL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have indeed looked into the matter. I can report to the House that the Government was advised of the circumstances relating to this case for the first time by the RCMP in 1977. At this time it was advised there was insufficient evidence to found a prosecution either under the Official Secrets Act or under the Criminal Code.
I would also remind Hon. Members that the matter was referred to indirectly by the McDonald Commission, which was fully aware of it, but that the McDonald Commission, with all of its recommendations about prosecutions and references to Attorneys General, made no recommendation that any prosecution be launched in connection with that matter.
November 10, 1982

subtopic: TRIAL OF BRITISH CIPHER CLERK-POSSIBLE CONSEQUENCES TO CANADA
TRIAL OF BRITISH CIPHER CLERK-POSSIBLE CONSEQUENCES TO CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question also relates to a security matter. This morning in a British court a British cipher clerk was convicted on seven charges of selling information to the Soviet bloc. He was sentenced to 35 years in prison. This is a great distinction from the policy of this Government, which has never yet charged a Canadian civil servant, although there have been many cases of traitorous activity over the years by civil servants in this country.
The Canadian Government uses the Cheltenham Communications Centre, not only for monitoring communications but also for the transmission of certain high level secret coded information. Would the Solicitor General assure the House that his British counterpart has assured him that there has been no breach of any Canadian security matter, and that no reforms are to take place now as a result of the revelations in a British court?

subtopic: TRIAL OF BRITISH CIPHER CLERK-POSSIBLE CONSEQUENCES TO CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to answer the premise before dealing with the question. When a possible piece of betrayal or treachery comes to the attention of the Government of Canada in connection with an individual, whether a public servant or not, I would remind Hon. Members that, while it is important justice be done in the case and that the individual be brought to justice, there are other considerations. In particular, the bringing forward of the case could very well compromise some ongoing activity of the security service, some legitimate activity, which is not made public for very good reasons, and it could betray sources which have furnished useful information to the security service. The important thing in that connection is that the penetration, if there has been one, or the betrayal, if there is one, be detected, that it be stopped, and that it be countered.
So far as the matter that took place in Britain today is concerned, I would want to assure the House that there is the closest co-operation between the security service of the RCMP and friendly security services of other countries. Penetration of any of them is a matter of common interest. There are policies in place, of which my hon. friend is aware. I can assure him that they are still in place to assure that intelligence service share information which is of benefit to all of them.

Madam Speaker, may I simply ask the Solicitor General why, from March 22, 1982, since presumably he had notice that these questions were
Oral Questions
on the Order Paper touching upon these very matters, including the one specifically referred to in the McDonald Commission report, the Government has not seen fit all these months, at least to name this traitor, and if the Government is not going to prosecute him, to see to it that something be done so he could at least receive the opprobrium, or otherwise, of Canadians for this treasonous act? Why is the Government protecting people such as this?

Madam Speaker, I would like to remind Hon. Members at this point, since my friend has characterized conduct as a treasonous act, that the matter is now before the Department of Justice. Until a prosecutorial decision is made, I think it is very unhelpful for Members of this House, or for the media, to characterize this behaviour in a way which might even prevent a fair trial from taking place. The matter has been referred to the Department of Justice. I have nothing further to say about it. I hope that other Members will bear in mind the damage that they can do to justice by making unjustified statements prematurely, or at all.

run jobs over the next 18 months, which means approximately

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by indicating that the Program that was announced in the economic statement two weeks ago was designed as a Program to attract further money into it. I wish he would read it, rather than read a resume prepared for him by a research staff which is in obvious need of some retraining. What we did point out in that particular study is that, while people are exhausting benefits, many of those who exhaust those benefits find jobs within the first seven or eight weeks after they have exhausted them. Therefore, we have used this Program to target the hardest hit cases in order to provide them with the alternative of going to work rather than welfare. That was the design of the Program. That is what the Program will meet.
I say to the Minister that, unlike Ministers of the Crown, people on this side of the House actually read their own reports and do not rely on resumes.

Madam Speaker, since the Minister has referred to his own report will he confirm that, in the report that he has just alluded to, a majority of those coming off unemployment insurance benefits will get no other benefit and will not get a job from his NEED Program even if we have additions made by provincial governments. Will he confirm that? Will he have the honesty to say that in the House of Commons?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a simple matter of record and it is in the report. When we presented the report we indicated that we are trying to identify a very serious issue. combine the best efforts of all those who are concerned about the problem.
We indicated that about 35 per cent to 40 per cent of those who finished their benefits do find alternate employment. Another 30 per cent or 40 per cent in that category have alternative forms of income, go back to school, or are parts of families where there are other wage earners. A group of about 10 per cent are those who have no alternative but to go on welfare or find alternative employment. We have targeted our Program specifically to that group.
I point out at the same time that we are also spending close to $560 million on other employment programs that are designed to help young people and women who are not in that category. We also have training programs that are providing places for a quarter of a million Canadians. This Department and the Government are providing a wide range of alternatives for those affected by the recession, because we do care.

Madam Speaker, the fact remains, for all those who were listening with care to what the Minister had to say, that over half of those coming off unemployment insurance benefits will not have any specific job program allocated for them. That is the reality, if you look carefully at the implications of the statistics that the Minister was rattling off.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The outcry following the November budget and the tax reform that was involved in that budget is the clearest indication that we can have that the tax changes introduced in that budget, which had such a damaging effect for small businesses and others, will have a damaging effect on the economy as well. Madam Speaker, I think it is quite obvious. I believe that across the country people in the business sector generally feel that they would rather spend all their energies trying to get the economy moving again rather than paying accountants and lawyers to advise them on brand new schemes of tax reform. I was not considering embarking upon any wholesale reform of taxation at the present time. 1 think that would be adding to uncertainty and creating exactly the kind of environment that my hon. friend does not want.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTRODUCE PRODUCTIVITY INCENTIVES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the new Minister of Finance. I would like to begin by congratulating him for taking on a very tough portfolio during a very difficult period, and 1 assure him that I wish him well.
As the OECD in its July economic survey devoted to Canada said, and I quote:
During the 1970s, Canadian manufacturing had the poorest productivity performance of ail of the 16 OECD countries with the absolute value of output per employee in 1980 some 23 per cent below the OECD weighted average.
My question to the Prime Minister is: in view of that situation, will he give serious consideration to introducing productivity incentives to be paid in direct proportion to increases in productivity in order that we may lower costs and selling prices and thereby increase sales and jobs, making it possible for people to find a job, taking them off the unemployment insurance rolls and enabling them to begin paying income tax once again? In my view, this process will make it possible to have the program start paying for itself very soon after it is initiated.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTRODUCE PRODUCTIVITY INCENTIVES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would first thank the Hon. Member for his good wishes, but he has gone a little bit too far by calling me Prime Minister in his question. I rejoice with him about the evolution of some factors in the economic indicators, particularly the fact that today the bank rate has gone down 36 points. The bank rate in Canada has gone down for 13 weeks in a row. That augurs well for interest rates in the next few months.
As far as his specific question is concerned, indeed Canada has a lot to catch up with in terms of productivity. Our record in the last few years has not been good. We have to do a lot better in the future than we have done in the past. I am certainly ready to examine his proposals in terms of a forthcoming budget. If he has some more specific way of putting his proposal into effect, I would like him either to write or talk to me. I would like to pursue this matter with him. His suggestion of increasing productivity is one that will indeed be a very high priority in any future budget, in fact in any economic step that the Government takes in the next few months.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS MATERIALS BY ROAD
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. The Minister will no doubt be aware of the serious accident which occurred on the Queen Elizabeth Highway between Hamilton and Niagara Falls in which a transport carrying flammable and dangerous materials went off the road, not only tying up traffic but being a cause of considerable potential damage. The Minister of Transport for the Province of Ontario said that he cannot promulgate his regulations governing the transportation of hazardous materials until the federal Government brings forward its regulations. When will the federal Government put its regulations out for discussion, and when will they in fact become law?

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF HAZARDOUS MATERIALS BY ROAD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have been in touch very recently with Mr. Snow, and the Minister of Transportation of Ontario has shown a lot of understanding of the difficulties of my department in writing these regulations. It has come to a point now where a judgment is developing in my Department that it might be a good idea to finalize the first unit of the regulations that have been Gazetted, and this may be the road I am going to take. I shall have to make my decision in the coming hours on that
November 10, 1982

particular subject. As for the finalization of the whole batch of regulations, 1 am afraid we expect to spend another year or so before this is done.

What is it about establishing or writing the regulations that requires such a long period of time? What will you know in two years that is not currently available by way of general knowledge as it affects the transportation of hazardous material? Does the Minister understand that on that particular highway we are looking at a disaster? One day the accident which occurs will not simply be a truck in a ditch. It will involve hundreds of other vehicles. Surely to God we do not have to wait another year or so for regulations protecting people against the transportation of hazardous materials.

Mr. Snow is obviously much better informed than my hon. friend on that subject because he does understand. There are a great many reconciliations which have to be made to regulations which exist now at the federal and provincial levels and regulations in the United States, with which we trade so much. There are regulations by international bodies which we also have to take into account. My hon. friend should get first-class information on that particular subject, and I will arrange that.
To come back to the specific accident which happened yesterday, the truck involved in it did, just by way of illustration, not have a placard, and the rules which are ready for implementation now do include those concerning placards. In other words, if that part of the Section, which is ready to go now, had been made law, it would have influenced that particular aspect of the accident. That is why I am considering dividing the package and implementing the first unit as soon as I can.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, November 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cosgrove (for Mr. MacEachen) that Bill C-130, to authorize continuing financial assistance to be provided to certain international financial institutions, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to complete my remarks on Bill C-130. There is a Clause which is causing considerable concern to us on this side. I am referring to Clause 4, an amendment to the schedule. Any changes will be done by Governor in Council, the Order in Council method which we do not approve of. We feel that Clause should be changed so that it will be the Parliament of Canada which will make any changes, not a Liberal Order in Council. I hope that issue is going to be dealt with in committee.
Now, I would just like to give some examples of what is happening with international banks such as the World Bank. The operational budget of the World Bank participants is combined because they share the same work force, administrative and overhead expenses. For the fiscal year 1981, the World Bank's administrative budget was $392 million. For purposes of comparison, the budget for the fiscal year 1976 was $185 million, $213 million in 1977, almost $246 million in 1978, $276 million in 1979, and for the fiscal year 1980 it was $338 million, which is a dramatic increase over the years.
What has caused some concern here and in the U.S. is that the bank has very high travel expenses, which have been the source for some critical comment. For the fiscal year 1981 the
November 10, 1982

bank has a travel budget of $43.4 million. In fiscal year 1980, the comparable amount was $38.7 million. That is an exorbitant amount for the World Bank to be using for travelling and it shows another reason why the concerns of the Canadian public should be listened to more closely in regard to foreign aid and how our money is handled.
It is worthy of comment, Mr. Speaker, that never in the 35-year history of the World Bank has there been any hint of irregularity or scandal when billions of dollars have been disbursed. Such a history runs counter to the entire human experience. In fact the Bank, in its reports, deplores the lack of uniform accounting practices and competent managers among borrowing nations. The true significance is reminiscent of Sherlock Holmes' observation in Conan Doyle's "Silver Blaze", that the clue lay in the failure of the hound to bay. The purity by silence of the World Bank's operations probably exists because those in a position to learn of irregularities might be personally embarrassed by such revelations.
It is also important, Mr. Speaker, to keep in mind that the IFIs lend directly to governments. In the case of developing countries, most of these governments are repressive and dictatorial. Corruption and mismanagement of the economy are far too common. Since cash loans especially will be placed in the general revenue of these governments, the opportunity for abuse becomes far greater. So I just want to remind the House that we are going to be spending $1.7 billion on foreign aid this year and we are very concerned that a very high percentage of that amount is being wasted through mismanagement and heaven only knows what else.
I would like to pay tribute to the Citizens for Foreign Aid Committee, Mr. Speaker, which is an Ontario based organization which does excellent research into foreign aid. They have come up with a lot of horror stories on waste and mismanagement with regard to foreign aid. In one of their recent newsletters they describe a horror story in Haiti. The Haitian project was a sorry mess of wholesale waste, local corruption and featherbedding, all funded by the Canadian taxpayer. Gerald Utting of The Toronto Star reported that the project was launched in 1974 with a sociological study by the Canadian International Development Agency which cost $800,000. Since 1974 CIDA has spent $24 million on the project, and to the naked eye there is precious little to show for it. The Haitian government failed to supply land for irrigation projects despite its commitment to do so. Transportation equipment and earth-moving machinery intended to be used strictly by DRIPP was taken over by Haitians for other uses. That is an example of the waste of foreign aid. The Haitians refused to give an account of how they were spending the money supplied to them for DRIPP projects. The Canadians were not able to find out exactly how many people were actually on the DRIPP payroll. A "W-5" program, aired earlier this year, showed a small local health clinic which cost a staggering $100,000 for new roofing. This, the commentator wryly noted, in a land where $2 a day is good wages. That is an example of where the Canadian taxpayer ends up being the drip in having to pay for this sort of project.
Financial Institutions
Last year, for example, the EDC decided to put up more than $160 million to finance a pulp and paper mill in Poland. It did this despite the fact that our own pulp and paper industry is struggling to stay alive in the face of fierce competition abroad, and despite the fact that everyone, including the Government, expects the Poles to be one of our major competitors in the European pulp and paper market. EDC rationalized this decision by pointing out that Poland would buy Canadian equipment for the plant, but this just does not hold up. In a state-run society the Polish worker is paid far less than his Canadian counterpart and ultimately Poland will be able to sell paper products far below Canadian prices. Our pulp and paper industry, which is only operating at 75 per cent capacity now, will shrink even further with fewer and fewer jobs for Canadian workers. So we have legitimate concerns, Mr. Speaker, and these are just examples of why this Bill should not be rushed through the House in too big a hurry.
To carry on with the horror stories, there is another example of $47 million going to the United States. I was not aware that the United States was an impoverished country. EDC announced last summer that it would put up $47 million for a mini-steel mill in Perth Amboy, New Jersey. This brings to $100 million the amount Canadian taxpayers have loaned for steel mills in St. Paul, Minnesota; Midlothian, Texas; Sheerness, England; and now New Jersey. In the meantime our own steel industry in Ontario and Nova Scotia is encountering stiff competition and the prospect of further lay-offs in Atlantic Canada where unemployment is already alarming and threatens to erupt in street violence. We are sending $47 million down to New Jersey. 1 am delighted that a Canadian firm got the contract for the New Jersey plant, but surely there is plenty of financing available in the United States. Surely it is not necessary to provide low-cost loans at the expense of our own industry, which is quite literally desperate for capital funds to upgrade its facilities.
There will have to be more parliamentary scrutiny of CIDA and foreign aid programs. Clause 4 must be amended so that Parliament can make changes to Bill C-130, rather than this being done by Order in Council.
I hope that when the Bill goes to Committee Clause 4 will be dealt with, the Order in Council ruling removed and Parliament given control of further foreign aid expenditures and moneys for CIDA.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had to consult my calendar today to be sure that yesterday was not Christmas and today the second day of Christmas. I suppose the public is to be spared four more days of what would be the same kind of largesse extended by this Parliament on behalf of international financial institutions. If evidence was ever needed that when this place is not functioning, taxpayers are sometimes better served, the occurrences in the last two days, including the Bill before the House today, would prove this.
Yesterday we went through the process of either extending direct financial contributions or extending demand promissory

November 10, 1982
Financial Institutions
notes, which have become encumbrances upon the people of Canada to the extent that $1,703,810,000 or over $1,000 million in foreign aid.
The argument has been made and will be made now with regard to the way Bill C-130 is drafted that what we are concerned with in large measure is a small contribution in cash, followed by a demand note to be used to raise money in some way by the financial institutions listed on the schedule to this Bill. The illusion that is created that these promissory notes do not constitute a liability against the Government of Canada and accordingly imposed upon the people of Canada is just that, an illusion. Just as any promissory note executed by any Member of the House constitutes a genuine liability, so does the execution of a promissory note or the execution of a demand note as contemplated by this legislation create a liability to be discharged. Those are the issues before the House.
On October 27, upon our return from our summer or fall recess, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) made the following statement, which is found at page 20078 of Hansard:
The world-wide recession has cut our economy to the bone. We have lost half a million jobs during the past year. Almost a million and a half among us are looking for work. Many others have temporarily given up the search for gainful employment. Virtually no Canadian has been untouched by the recession. In every region of the country, those who have been spared the worst have relatives, friends or neighbours who are struggling to cope with hardship and insecurity- be they unemployed textile workers in Quebec, grounded fishermen in the Atlantic Provinces, idle lumbermen in British Columbia, laid off miners or auto workers in Ontario.
That is a rare group of people in terms of numbers and in terms of occupation, Mr. Speaker. Compared to the calamities referred to on October 27, with what are we faced today?
Despite the clamouring of the New Democratic Party for more assistance for the unemployed, it is very interesting to find that there is not a Member of that Party present in the House at the moment ready to deal with this issue. They have run away from the frightening prospect of being accused of providing additional funds abroad, when there is not enough money in Canada to look after the needs to which reference was made by the Minister of Finance on October 27.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Of course there are NDP Members present in the House. We are waiting for a Progressive Conservative to speak on this matter.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know the purpose of that intervention, other than to permit me to indicate that the Member who intervened was not in the House at the time I made the comment. I would point out that he is the only Member of that Party in the House ready to deal with these essential issues.
I should like to deal with the terms of the Bill before us. Clause 3 reads as follows:
The Secretary of State for External Affairs may, for the purpose of promoting the social and economic development of developing countries, provide financial assistance to an institution by way of
(a) direct payments to the institution;
(A) the issuance to the institution of non-interest bearing, non-negotiable demand notes in a form determined by the Minister of Finance; and
(c) the purchase on behalf of Her Majesty in right of Canada of shares of the institution.
The "institution" is one of a number of institutions listed in the schedule attached to the Bill. Clause 6, which is the operative Clause giving rise to the commitment of the Government, reads as follows:
In respect of the period between the date this Act comes into force and March 31, 1983,
(a) there is hereby appropriated for the purposes of paragraph 3(a), the sum of four hundred and forty-two thousand dollars to be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund from time to time as required; and
(A) the amount of financial assistance provided to institutions pursuant to paragraph 3(A) shall not exceed the equivalent of one hundred and seventeen million, forty thousand dollars.
The total amount under the operative Clause is $117,482,000. It is significant that that commitment is for a relatively brief period, less than five months from the date the Bill is passed until the end of March, 1983. I do not think my mathematics are incorrect, Mr. Speaker. If we take the average, we are authorizing a commitment of $23,496,400 per month at a time when it is extremely difficult to get the Government to make any funds available for the general relief of poverty and depression in Canada.
Yesterday we had the pleasure of listening to an explanation of the way in which the astronomical sum of $1,703,810,000 was to be dealt with in terms of financial aid to foreign financial institutions. One of the arguments made by the Minister responsible for the introduction of the Bill related to the demand note nature of the commitment. The allegation made to the House was that we should not be too concerned because the vast majority of those sums, indeed 92.5 per cent, were to be secured only by demand notes. In fact, the Government of Canada was not reaching into the Consolidated Revenue Fund at this time for the purpose of extracting that substantial sum of money but was only putting up 7.5 per cent of it in cash and hopefully would never be called upon to pay the balance. However, it is significant to note that yesterday I asked the Minister, in a series of questions, what the total actual commitment of the Government of Canada was under Bill C-129, and he confirmed in the House that the total commitment was the amount referred in the Bill which, when totalled, exceeded $2 billion.
The same must be said today, having regard to the same general method employed in providing either cash or a security, which is an encumbrance upon the assets of Canada for the purpose of funding foreign aid as contemplated by this piece of legislation. It may be comforting to the Government to suggest that of the total amount of $117,482,000, the trifling, inconsequential and insignificant sum of only $442,000 is to be laid out immediately. Regardless of all the arguments which may be made on any side of the House with respect to the method of financing these commitments, to my mind $442,000 today is a substantial sum of money; but linked as it is to the
November 10, 1982

further obligation to issue demand notes for $117,040,000, I think it is a frightening thing that the House does not have a full complement of Members who can direct their attention to this matter and, as the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) urged, find in the Bill the funds they would like used for the purpose of creating jobs in Canada.
