subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
I am inclined to ask how the Bill fits into the financial scheme of things that appear in Part 1 of the 1982-83 Estimates. I am referring to page 33 thereof where we find that the total official development assistance established by the Government is fixed at $1,724 million. Of that amount, according to the same page, we find that the investment and advances to international financial institutions-value of cash and notes to be issued-totals only $332 million.
Yesterday we passed a Bill with respect to financial institutions for the amount of $1,703,810,000. We are now asked to pass this Bill which adds $117,482,000 to the same amount, an amount which quite frankly exceeds the amount that appears in the Estimates. But the matter does not end there. If we refer once again to the speech of the Minister of Finance on October 27, as reported at page 20083 of Hansard, we note that he has taken the unusual step of reducing the amount of development aid. He said:
Outlays in the areas of defence and official development assistance will be reduced by $230 million and $245 million respectively from the dollar levels previously allocated.
The mathematics are simply not there to support the position. Within a period of two days the House has already
Financial Institutions
approved amounts with respect to bilateral foreign aid through investment and advances to financial institutions which exceed, in their amount, the entire amount of development assistance referred to in the Estimates. Unfortunately, when the Minister delivered his non-budget speech on October 27, we did not have the benefit of an accompanying financial analysis of from where these funds were in fact to come or what the consequential results of the reduction in these various budgetary items might be.
If I may return to a rather interesting aspect of the Bill itself, there is a provision whereby the "Governor in Council may, by order, amend the schedule" by adding names thereto or deleting names therefrom. What Parliament is asked to do, accordingly, is to grant to the Government of Canada the right to spend, in essence, $117,482,000 in whatever fashion it pleases.
Having given them the right to add to the schedule or to take from the schedule-and I might say that the only power they really needed was the power to add since they had the power to allocate among those institutions referred to in the schedule-I can imagine the circumstance where one of the other financial institutions which might be added would be the special Swiss trust account of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), because there is nothing to prevent the Government from adding any financial institution it might wish to add on using the entire amount to put into whatever financial institution it might wish. They are not only banks referred to in the schedule, but funds. Any fund which the Government might wish to create or subscribe to would qualify, and the House will have lost the opportunity to intervene and ask whether the moneys have been well spent. We do not know what one dime of these funds will be used for, not one dime. All we know is that we are asked to give authority to the Government to put the money into the fund or into the Bank.
Let me read into the record some of the institutions referred to in the Schedule: the African Development Fund, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Fund and the Asian Development Bank. The significant issue is that without any input from Parliament, any other fund either now in existence or to be brought into existence later may be added to the list. Every dime of the $117,482,000 may be put into that fund. We are not told the purposes of the expenditures of the fund or the Bank. The whole matter is left to our imagination; I might say not to very close scrutiny in terms of the manner which this House has hitherto dealt with this Bill.
It is my submission that this House ought not to approve a financial request by Government to spend money in whatever fashion it desires, which is exactly what this Bill would permit.
My concern is that with a budgetary deficit this year projected by the Minister of Finance to exceed $23 billion, probably reaching $25 billion, with interest on the national debt to be paid this year alone in the projected amount of

Financial Institutions
$16.4 billion and with the Government having borrowed over $21 billion, is it prudent for the Government to borrow money in order to give it away?
Let me ask some rather basic elementary questions. Would an individual citizen borrow money to give it away? Would Members of this House as individuals borrow money to give it away? If not, why as representatives of our constituents do we come here and authorize the disbursement freely of moneys owned, claimed by the people of Canada, in a give-away project when, at the same time, we are saddling these same Canadians with an obligation to pay their pro rata share of some $16 billion in interest? The obligation with respect to these programs is not one that will end with us. Very clearly, our children will be able to carry on the great tradition of paying for the debts that we have created and for which we are responsible.
I wonder how that whole process fits into the scheme of the just society. Is it just and reasonable for people in this place today to load our children and our grandchildren with obligations that they will have to pay for tomorrow? I hardly think so. I hardly think that is appropriate. Yet this is exactly what we are doing. No reasonable, prudent Member of this House would undertake a personal action of the kind the Government is undertaking. I think therein lies one of the great problems of the Government and of the House itself. We have not come to grasp the significance of the money in our charge.
I practise law, as some others in this House do, and we have trust accounts that we in a law practice administer. Those accounts are used for the prupose of depositing funds that do not belong to us. They are not funds to which a law firm can claim title, subject of course to the fact that we can extract funds from that account to pay for services that are rendered. But the balance of those funds, whatever they amount to, are subject to the call of the person who owns the money therein. The funds can be paid out on the individual's direction or for the individual's benefit.
Looking at the Consolidated Revenue Fund, is there any difference between that fund, for which we have a responsibility, and a normal trust fund that I have just described? The answer is that there is not. We are charged with the responsibility to attend to the interests of the people who have worked hard and have had extracted from their salaries or from the pockets of their business an amount that is contributed to this fund, from which the Government extracts all.
I had an opportunity on the weekend to have a discussion with an officer of the Department of National Revenue. He indicated to me that his responsibility was to attend at the various businesses within my riding and examine the accounts that had fallen into default, accounts of taxpayers, many of which related to trust money. We are all acquainted with the provisions of the Income Tax Act and the Canada Pension Plan which oblige employers to extract from the salaries of their employees amounts by way of a withholding tax representing weekly or monthly shares of their salary which are taxed. The tax goes into a fund and on the fifteenth of each
November 10, 1982
month is paid to the Receiver General for Canada, including an amount with respect to Canada Pension Plan contributions and unemployment insurance contributions by both employer and employee. What he has found, unfortunately, and it is not unusual, is that employers have been using these trust funds to carry on their daily activities. The only reason for that is that they desperately need every dollar they can find in order to survive. There is no excuse under the law for this practice. Unfortunately, this practice is growing and it is growing in these severe economic times.
The Crown recognizes that those moneys are trust funds so-called, and many Canadians have been prosecuted for dipping in, as it were, to the trust funds. I then asked what happens when those trust funds become part of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. The answer was that any semblance of their being a duty or a trust has vanished. There is no obligation upon the Government of Canada to continue to administer those funds, in the same fashion that there was an obligation upon the individual taxpayer to administer and take charge and care of those funds. I submit that we in this place should reflect upon our duties with respect to these moneys which today we are asked to lavish on financial institutions to be spent, once they are handed to these institutions, in whatever fashion they may prefer.
Let me deal with one of those institutions referred to in the Schedule, one to which 1 have already made reference, namely the African Development Bank. That Bank has a project for the construction of a rail link north of the Republic of South Africa to permit the produce from Zambia and other nations to be transported to the east or the west coast of the African continent without the need to transport goods over the territory of the Republic of South Africa. That is an objective which is, in the minds of those who are determined to build the line, an improvement over the existing circumstances. There is one great problem. When that line passes through Mozambique it is subject to regular guerrilla attacks. When the line passes through Angola, it is subject to regular guerrilla attacks by the UNITA movement in that country.
While I do not know if that is the purpose of the expenditure of those funds, the consequence is that the money will surely be wasted. It is a sink hole. As long as these states through which the railway is to pass cannot control their own domestic population, there is no valid reason why money should be spent on a project like that. We do not even know whether that is the project because we have not been given any information and we never will have any information. It does indicate to me, however, that without the Government coming before Parliament and identifying the purpose, the quantum and all normal ancillary information referable to this matter, Parliament should reject the request out of hand.
A petition was filed in the House today urging that no additional foreign aid be extended to Tanzania. The petition was signed by certain residents of the Province of Ontario and
November 10, 1982

was submitted to the House by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). The petition referred to the dictatorial Marxist government of that country. There was reference to the expropriation without compensation of business enterprises that were owned by Canadians. What assurances does the House have that the African Development Fund or the African Development Bank will not advance funds to Tanzania, a country where some of these actions referred to by the petitioners apparently occur?
When dealing with this Bill Hon. Members should be cognizant of a number of circumstances. First, it is part of an over-all international development program for foreign aid. In light of our pressing financial circumstances, would it not be appropriate for the House to undertake an examination of the rules by which this Government would extend aid to foreign nations? Is it not now appropriate to refer this entire matter to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence for an in depth examination of the principles that should lie behind the extension of foreign aid? This is something which 1 recommended to the then Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister some time ago.
I am convinced that there are millions of Canadians who recognize, in view of these substantial sums of money advanced and guaranteed, that there should be some pressing issue for the benefit of Canadians that should override the natural inclination of the Government to make these funds available to create jobs and assure security for Canadians. Do we not owe them the obligation to investigate this matter in its entirety and develop some general rules?
1 would like to suggest some rules that might be applied in determining how foreign aid should be extended. 1 do not believe that it is uncumbent upon us as a nation to engage in a type of international socialist redistribution of wealth because there are nations that are less prosperous than us. Invariably we will find that all we have done is redistribute the poverty. I heard the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) confirm in the House yesterday that citizens in certain foreign countries would gladly exchange their good times for our bad times. I recognize that fact.
However, what is the purpose behind our foreign aid program? It should be to create a climate in the nations which receive those funds that will give rise to the creation of national wealth within their own boundaries. This will not occur until those nations have governments which are freely elected under a system which permits opposition parties to seek election in a social and judicial circumstance which grants universal human rights to all their citizens.
I realize that Members to my left have complained about the extension of any foreign aid to Guatemala. At the same time they clamour for additional foreign aid to Nicaragua. It is not a coincidence, of course, that the government they wish to receive this aid should be dominated by a Marxist leaning government and that the government to which they oppose giving aid is one which is against Marxist government in Nicaragua.
I submit to the House that the test should be an objective one without regard to ideological leanings. Countries should be
Financial Institutions
asked if they grant universal human rights to their citizens and, in fact, permit opposition parties, in a free and democratic election, to form a democratic legislature which is supported by a democratically elected executive.
What is the cause of the poverty in many of these nations? My colleague the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche) directed his attention to this issue and confirmed that people in the Third World are in worse economic circumstances today than they were before, despite all the foreign aid which has been extended in the past. What does that signal to us? Is it our obligation to increase the expenditure? Should we be engaged in a program which provides for massive injections into it from our depleted assets?
Let us examine the circumstances which exist in those countries. There are countries which have dictatorships. There are regimes which suppress the free enterprise system which has given rise to the wealth that we enjoy today, subject to the diminution to which reference has been made over recent years. Nevertheless, the system was in place but it is not now in place in those nations. Therefore, our first objective should be to tie our foreign aid to commitments by the nations receiving same to accept the principles to which I have just made reference. In the absence of those commitments, I suggest that the foreign aid should no longer be extended except in cases where there has been a natural disaster that has unexpectedly claimed lives and created havoc within the boundaries of those individual sovereign states.
As we approach the time for close consideration and a vote on these matters, I urge my colleagues on all sides of the House to consider, apart from what may have been the thrust in foreign policy and the drive to additional and excessive foreign aid grants in the past, whether it is not appropriate to consider the needs of their own constituents and Canadians generally in light of today's circumstances.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to intervene in this debate but, after listening to the arguments advanced by the Hon. Member for York North (Mr. Gamble), I thought 1 would address this issue, if only for a short while, and put some of my ideas formally on the record.
The first thing I would like to say is that I basically approach this matter from the same perspective as the Hon. Member for York North; that is, I think that, if we will be spending such large sums of money, we should ensure that those sums will create jobs for Canadians. Therefore, I do not want to take exception to those parts of his remarks which were addressed to job creation in Canada.
What I would like to point out to him, though, is that his argument is not unlike the spurious arguments of many Canadians who ask the question: If we are to spend $1 billion, $2 billion or more, why, in Heaven's name, would the Government spend the money abroad on other people? Why, in a time of difficulty, do we not spend the money here on Canadian industry, on Canadian businessmen, to produce Canadian profits and Canadian jobs? I think that argument blithely

November 10, 1982
Financial Institutions
ignores the basic reality of the Canadian economy of the 1970s and the 1980s.
The Hon. Member surely knows, and those Canadians who believe or accept his argument should know, that Canada is one of the greatest trading nations of the world today. Thirty per cent of everything we produce is sold abroad. If that is the case-if we do sell so many of our goods and services abroad, and if that market is 100 times larger than our domestic market-then surely we should be able to see that a dollar invested in the foreign market should produce results which are potentially 100 times greater than if the same dollar were invested in our domestic market. In short, I would argue, and I would want others to believe, that if we are to create jobs for Canadians, now and in the future, the best opportunity we have of creating them is in those areas which export to the foreign market.
If you accept the argument, Mr. Speaker, that it is better to spend money in developing export markets for Canadian products, then the next question is: Where would these exports markets be developed? I think most of us understand that our primary export market is in the United States. 1 think it takes something like two-thirds of all the goods we produce and about 80 per cent of all the manufactured goods. That means that, in part, the United States will continue to be the major focus of our export market in the near future. But where does the opportunity for significant expansion over the long term really exist? I suggest that any Hon. Member of the House who has read the minutes of the parliamentary task force on the National Trading Corporation will have discovered that Japan, West Germany and ail of our major competitors among the OECD countries have concluded, after considerable research, that the market of the future lies in the developing countries of the Pacific Rim and South America and in those countries that we describe as Third World nations.
Having identified those areas as our future markets, members will have found that our trading competitors are not afraid to spend money abroad, unlike the Hon. Member for York North and many of his colleagues. Those nations are prepared to spend large sums of money on developing Third World nations for two reasons. First, they understand that, to a degree, the expenditure of funds purchases good will in those communities. Second, the expenditure of sizeable sums of money in those countries primes the pump of the national economies of those nations. As they build themselves, as they enrich their economies, they are increasingly able to purchase the sophisticated and more expensive consumer goods from the Japanese homeland and European markets.
Therefore, unlike some Hon. Members of the House and unlike many Canadians-some of them my constituents-I am not afraid to spend money in the poorer parts of the world. Despite their political systems, whatever the social arrangements they may be in the process of working out, I am not afraid to spend money in those countries because I think that ultimately, given time, proper advice and guidance from countries such as Canada and others in the western democratic
industrialized world, those countries will develop into extremely prosperous recipients of Canadian primary and manufactured products. Therefore, to ignore those countries now, to turn our backs on them for whatever reason, would be to commit the ultimate folly and doom us to the slowest growth we could ever witness as a nation since the Second World War.
Finally, I would like to inform the Hon. Member who last spoke and those who may share his thoughts that Hon. Members on this side are not without critical faculties. Many of us have discussed foreign aid among ourselves and have reached certain conclusions, some of which I would like to share this afternoon.
There are three criticisms I would offer in a very general way. First, instead of spending less than we are spending now, I think we should be spending considerably more. Second, before we enrich our foreign aid program, we should have an independent committee of inquiry to find out just how efficiently the present policies are delivering our money and assistance to the recipient countries today. That committee may be the present External Affairs Committee, one of its subcommittees, or, better still, a special task force of the House, since task forces have revealed an ability to work quickly and with considerable insight, two characteristics which would lend themselves to this sort of inquiry.
Finally, I hope that before too long the Government of Canada, by itself, in co-operation with the business community or with provincial Governments, will create institutions or shape attitudes which will allow Canadian businessmen to exploit more aggressively foreign markets than at present. For every dollar that we contribute to foreign aid, Canadian businessmen receive roughly 15 or 16 cents back by way of foreign contracts. Compare that with the Japanese who get back roughly $2.40 for every dollar they invest in foreign aid. One can see there is a desperate need for Canadian business and for Canadian Governments at both levels to generate one strategy or another to ensure that any money we invest, aside from the humanitarian result that we all accept and honour in the expenditure of taxpayers' money, will generates the highest return for our businessmen and the highest number of jobs for our workers.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the previous speaker. One thing about debate in the House of Commons on a subject such as Canadian relations with the world, foreign aid and human aid, is that it encourages people who do not normally participate in external affairs and such issues to come forward with common sense and good ideas which might in fact be new to them but perhaps are not new to the House of Commons. I invite that Hon. Member to join the External Affairs Committee. He shows a positive human interest. He will find that we have had a considerable number of studies in the House of Commons and in committee on the North-South dialogue and other related issues. His contribution would be appreciated there and I look forward to seeing him in the future.
November 10, 1982

It does not matter from which corner of the House one comes, it is my opinion that all Members of the House of Commons start from the same basic premise that all men and all nations of good conscience want to improve the human condition, particularly as it relates to the poorest of the poor wherever they may be found in the world and regardless of their national boundary.
The spirit and will of Canadians to be generous, caring and giving is a matter of historical record. The method of assisting all individuals in the world first to survive and then to maximize their individual potential through development is where the separation of concepts begins to widen among all factions of the weak who have the need to receive and the strong who have the capacity and will to give.
This Bill is all about international financial institutions created by governments to tackle the problems of millions of individuals and governments who have proven not competent to survive and compete under current world inter-relationships and conditions. Unfortunately, the methods that the financial institutions that we currently strive to uphold in this Bill employ, as well-intentioned as they are and will be in the future, have to be assessed very carefully, because these institutions to which we will now be giving more money have failed in the world. In spite of these institutions the poor have become poorer and the numbers of poor have grown larger and larger.
The Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Roche), the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) and others have talked in this House about the physical and spiritual starvation existing throughout the world. Like many other Members, 1 stand here today and bear witness to man's inhumanity to man. I could stand in judgment against many nations of the world. In my speech today, I do not want to do that. I want to recognize that the world is not poor by nation, the world is poor by individuals. You can see poverty here in Canada, material poverty and hunger. You can also see spiritual poverty here in Canada. As I stand in the House today to illustrate, I will not be paternalistic.
About three years ago one of my constituents, at the time when Canada was open to a group of refugees, opened his home to a young refugee. This constituent is a very close friend of mine. In addition to opening his home, he found a job and a place in the community for this young person. Unfortunately, about a year ago this young person was killed in an automobile accident. He grieved for him as one of his own.
This man tried again. He took in another of the poor people from another nation and provided him with a home and opportunity in our economy. Last weekend two young Canadians on motorcycles saw this young man who was trying to make his way in Canada walking along the road. They got off their motorcycles, punched this young man, a young Vietnamese, into unconsciousness, threw him into the middle of the road, a car ran over him and he died.
What kind of poverty is that? It is the worst kind of poverty one can imagine. We have to attack that poverty of spirit. We have to stand behind the spirit of generosity that says: "I will take one of the poor of the world and give him an opportunity
Financial Institutions
in Canada". I feel just terrible for my country and in particular my own riding about the truth of that reality.
Poverty is not alone in this nation or any nation. No one has a monopoly on poverty or greed. Let us look at it in a world context. Poverty, wherever it is found, can be materialistic or of the spirit. If we are to change these things, we must generate a new ethic that stands on the basic value of production. The philosophy of the current institutions have failed to stop the slide of the world into further and further poverty. They have not stopped the poor from becoming poorer and poorer and larger in number. They will fail further unless they change their direction and basic philosophies. Their intention has been good, but their capacity has not been either efficient or competent to address the problem.
Current United Nations and international financial institutions to a great degree are mired in the philosophy of the redistribution of existing wealth and power. The method of redistribution of this existing wealth and power is seen to come through collectivism, instead of recognizing that the solution lies in the philosophy of creation and distribution of new wealth and new power, through the creation of new opportunities for individuals to generate growth and prosperity from within their individual being.
The redistribution ethic starts from the concept of the limits to growth. Assuming that wealth and power are finite and depleting, we must live basically-I realize there are degrees- within the existing parameters of wealth and power. The problem is not the creation of new wealth and power, but rather the redistribution of that wealth in the world today. This is a valid ethic. It is valid intellectually. It has value from a humanist point of view. It is all tied nicely together in the concept of consumption and environment. It recognizes that the world must control its consumption in some way, otherwise we will destroy the environment. It ties together, the no-growth theory very nicely with another broad theory, and that is the theory of socialism, the redistribution of existing wealth and power rather than the creation of new.
Another one of the problems is that this theory is unfortunately carried by the leaders of the world today. It comes out of older thought, from perhaps the London School of Economics and other such institutions where the leaders of the current world, of the new emerging worlds like Africa, obtained their education, values and ethics. 1 am not judging and saying it is wrong. There are many good things about it. It is just that that way of implementation is not going to work. The world is getting poorer and poorer under it. And that is a fact, not just a statement of opinion.
To solve the problem, the theory is we should begin with relief, and then we must provide development through the transfer of resources and technology, specifically, the layering on first of basic food, because a man that is hungry cannot work. Then the man with no shelter must have some form of basic shelter. He gets his food and shelter, but he cannot

November 10, 1982
Financial Institutions
participate in the world until he is educated and has proper health care. We must first set up a basic welfare program which will bring the people of the poor nations to a condition where they may begin to work to build their economy.
There is somehow an idea that social reform must precede economic development or economic reform. Unfortunately, it has been demonstrated that when social reform runs too far ahead rather than parallel with economic development, the latter in fact does not and will not occur, because the incentive to make it occur has been taken from the machinery of administration and from the basic value structure. This vertical development concept will never work because it ignores the basic elements of parallel value development which establishes, in conjunction with, or even prior to, programs which demonstrate opportunities for individual initiative and incentive which, in turn, ensure upward mobility through work, profit and individual enterprise.
North-South dialogue starts with the premise that wealthy nations of the North have all the resources and technology, all the wealth and power. The South, on the other hand, has all the poverty and lack of human and physical resources. The North-South dialogue which is bogged down now, is bound to be bogged down in failure because it was initiated on a false premise. Many of us have visited in the South. 1 wonder if any members of the committee of the House of Commons who travelled to Latin America, or anyone who saw that poverty, went hungry on their visit. 1 do not think any Member of this House of Commons, including myself, has ever really gone hungry, certainly not when we have visited the South, because as well as gross and abject poverty, there is also amongst these nations and their communities, opulent wealth and abundant unexploited resource potential.
There is in this world, Mr. Speaker, substantial wealth and power that remains untouched and undeveloped in the South. The poor exist in the North as the wealthy exist in the South. The poor exist as individuals in all nations, including our own. We must stop addressing poor nations, in our programs and start addressing poor individuals. We must attempt to create new opportunities for poor individuals wherever they are found. We need to identify nations which accept the values of the work ethic, individual initiative, and incentive, the profit motive, and enterprise and freedom. These values are the motors of productivity regardless of where they are found. This is the model which has proven successful and has generated the basic economy, not only for our nation but for all of the Western nations, and in fact, the greatest giving nations in the world.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: So why are we in a recession?

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
We are in a recession, Mr. Speaker, to answer my friend from New Westminster, because we, too, in this nation, have lost the concept of the work ethic, individual initiative, and incentive, and we also put down the profit motive and free entreprise which have created this nation. While we want to protect our humanistic values, we must still
support that economy, and this is the system which is successful throughout the world and the system we should be passing on to the Third World. We should not just be passing along material goods; we should be passing along the value system behind the aspect of real production. It used to be thought that in order to get production, you took a raw resource, added labour, then capital and technology, and you had production. But we have applied these things in many parts of the world and we did not get production because we forgot to apply one element. There will not be production if there is not incentive and profit. Therefore, we must get back to that reality. We must find nations that recognize the fact that in order to develop, or have development, they must face that reality. We should not keep pumping good money after bad into those nations that choose the collectivist socialist route, which has not and is not working. It has not and is not working anywhere in the world. Certainly, as humanists we must give basic relief, but if we want to move from relief to development, perhaps we had better choose those nations that want to move with the basic values which have generated the creative production of our society.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Like who?

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: The Hon. Member asks like who. I did not ask her to ask these questions resulting from my speech, but I appreciate it. That is my next answer. Like who? If we take areas of the world where we look at the situation and say it is hopeless, there is no way that this nation can develop, and then we put the enterprise ethic there, that is where the success story is. There is no development aid provided to Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan. In fact, the ones we have isolated and not provided development aid to have demonstrated the way to organize their society for greater success for the poorest of their poor.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: You are talking about American aid.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Well, there are different kinds of aid. There is a relief package and there is a development package, which is really just an extended relief package. It is just a redistribution.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Are you really talking about U.S. aid in Taiwan?

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Certainly, U.S. aid in Taiwan, U.S. economic development aid. I am in favour of it because that is what stimulates the economy and raises the poor up. Exactly. On this basis, Mr. Speaker, we are not going to have to go to committee, because the message is getting through to the other side.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: They said they did it on their own.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
They did it on their own, that is right, with economic development aid in the form of enterprise. And I am for developing that enterprise in all nations of the world. If we
November 10, 1982

would do that and export it to the developing countries, then we would start in fact to help them on the road to recovery.
There are those who claim that somehow those of the redistribution philosophy have some corner on humanism, human rights, freedom, liberation, democracy and free choice, and that somehow these values are the opposite of enterprise and the profit motive. There certainly seems to be that indication, because those who support the capitalist mode are in fact condemned and it is assumed that they could not possibly be humanists. Human rights, humanism, relief and development, in fact free democracies, are not the opposite of free markets and individual enterprise systems; they are the byproduct of these systems. A system which produces exists in a society with the greatest human rights. The society with the greatest humanists is that of a giving nation. They have relief, development and free democracy with free choice, and those come from the generation of wealth in a free market, the individual enterprise system.
What we have to do for Third World countries, Mr. Speaker, is to help them take their own potential wealth and make it grow so that they can meet their own needs as well as the needs of the poorest nations of the Third World. We can keep pouring more and more money into financial institutions in an attempt to redistribute it, but if redistribution is the value thrust rather than creation, the hole gets bigger and bigger and the poor grow poorer and poorer and more and more in numbers.
My constituents would want me to support this Bill, as 1 intend to, but they would feel more confident about the support 1 give this Bill if they felt somehow assured that in its passage the world would somehow be less poor, that there would in fact be success in putting a dent in international poverty. 1 wish 1 could believe, as I support this Bill, that this would be the case, but it will not happen until the institutions themselves rebuild from a new philosophy emphasizing the creation of wealth rather than redistribution. Wealth and power are not limited; they are as infinite as the capacity of the individual to live, grow and develop his own unlimited potential. Canada cannot survive and continue to grow unless we are a part of world institutions, striving to stabilize and lift international economic order. We have no choice with this Bill because without stability and economic order, even if it is wrongly oriented or directed, we have no world at all with no standard of living for anyone.
Aiding these institutions, Mr. Speaker, need not be based upon altruism and humanism alone. The poorest nations have no capacity to consume, to buy, to trade. Canada's standard of living is directly proportional to our capacity to trade. Our own economic welfare is sustained in uplifting the poor in the poorest regions of the world. There are many motivations for international aid, and while the loftiest of these might well be humanism, enlightened self-interest and mutual interest can be found in the establishment of development as equal reasons. For those on either side, whether they support foreign aid because of humanism or self interest, the reasons for supporting this Bill appear self-evident on that basis.
Financial Institutions
There are many things that we do not like about this Bill. We are becoming accustomed to finding in every Bill something which says: write me a blank cheque. Let the Government which knows better expand where it will. Let it have no accountability. That is what this Bill does, and that is an unfortunate part which will have to be removed. 1 as a Member of Parliament cannot grant to the Government of Canada the unlimited right to spend more. We are going to give the Government a right to a limit here, a limit which in itself we are stretching to reach. I cannot give beyond that limit. If Hon. Members opposite want my support on the Bill, they will have to consider that in committee and they will have to remove that order in council clause.
My good friend and colleague from the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence said he hoped that I would give a good, progressive speech. I hope my speech is progressive because it talks about creation of new wealth and power which can in fact lift the developing world. Canadians accept that the Government, on their behalf, should contribute a portion of their tax dollars to relief and development. Their greatest concern, however, is that their tax dollars are being wasted through poor administration, poor management and corruptive redistribution of wealth from our country to the corporate Government and the elite of poorer nations.
There are many ways that we as Canadians can help poor people and poor nations lift themselves into self-sufficiency and from there, hopefully, toward surplus production. Canada can give abundantly of its human resources. In our nation we keep cutting back our educational productivity. For example, school boards are not hiring teachers, they are laying off teachers, competent teachers. Health care facilities are cutting back and laying off nurses. They are laying off competent human resources. Instead of putting that human resource on unemployment insurance, why can we not take it and offer it to the developing world? This does not just apply to the teaching and health care areas. Even productive enterprise in our economy is cutting back, which has created a surplus of both management and labour. Instead of keeping this resource on hold, why not find a way of providing human resources which could help to build elsewhere? Not only would we be helping by taking this human resource to assist in the Third World, but in addition to that we would be providing a mutual benefit to a resource which has been put on hold through unemployment insurance in Canada. These people would gain a new benefit in the form of a second language, a second culture and new economic ideas. Therefore, it could be again a mutual interest in the sharing of the pool of human resources.
We talk constantly in terms of limiting production. We establish marketing boards which are supposed to sell, but they also limit. They maintain certain price levels. Why should we not encourage our people to produce as much as they can, sell as much of that production in the market and use the excess- excess production because we do not have an excess of capital? I know the Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) tries to do that, and we are great givers of food in the world from our surplus, and I think that is the kind of thing Canadians can

November 10, 1982
Financial Institutions
and should do. That is what we are best equipped to do. But 1 have to say that I do have some concern about giving more capital when we are in fact a capital-poor country ourselves. We are a developing country which needs that capital here, to develop and produce here, to teach the world to produce in a similar way and give them the excess of that production. Capital and credit have limits, Mr. Speaker. We are limited in the amount of capital and credit that this nation can extend, because we are overextended now. As people listen to this debate and hear us grant additional money and additional financial support to these international institutions and giving additional multilateral aid in the form of capital and credit, they will realize that we have reached a limit.
International institutions must recognize that further capitalization such as this has its limits. If there has been some acrimony in this debate, it will show the world the concern that is being expressed as we come near to that limit.
Before we become recipients of aid, rather than contributors to the institutions that we attempt to uphold today, we must stabilize our economy rather than further destabilize the economy of the world. It is difficult to balance things so as to know when to give and when not to give. When do we stabilize world economics and when do we stabilize our own? That balance must be found, Mr. Speaker, before Canadians become poorer and poorer and a larger part of the problem.
The North-South dialogue which expressed the problems of the North and South has become too much an "us" and "them" problem. It was wrong to divide things North and South rather than just poor people wherever they are found throughout the world, as individuals. In the dialogue of North-South, the object of the South seems to have been to try to put a guilt trip on the North. The North seems to feel guilty about the wealth it has generated and guilty for being successful in a material way. When we enter a dialogue we almost have to apologize for materialistic success.
I think we must stop having an inferiority complex regarding our own values. Why put down materialistic values when they are what generates economic development? Why assume that our social and cultural values are inferior? Let us not approach this subject with guilt; instead, let us uphold the values that have created this society.
It often happens that when we travel in older parts of the world we are told that we are good at making money, creating wealth, or creating production. People want to know how it is done. We have to show them how it is done, Mr. Speaker, and must transmit a different set of values as well as our concept of production, Mr. Speaker.
What I am about to say is not a statement that is new to this House, Mr. Speaker, and it has already been made all around the world. At the Cancun Conference President Reagan started talking along this line of thought, saying that it is time to stop developmental assistance coming in the guise of little more than the subsidization of social revolutions. We have to look at development in its correct context. We must give it a
very practical and hard look. I hope that hard look will begin again when the Bill reaches committee. I look forward to that active discussion over the next few weeks, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) CONTINUING ASSISTANCE ACT AUTHORIZATION OF CONTINUING FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to take part in this debate on Bill C-130, an Act to authorize continuing financial assistance to be provided to certain international financial institutions, namely, the African Development Fund, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Fund, the Asian Development Bank, the InterAmerican Development Bank, the Fund for Special Operations (InterAmerican Development Bank), the Caribbean Development Bank and the Special Development Fund, the International Fund for Agricultural Development and the Common Fund for Commodities.
If I am not mistaken, Mr. Speaker, this is the First such debate to be held in this House. I am very much in favour of it and I congratulate the government for giving us the opportunity to have a debate on this issue.

May I begin this part of my speech, Mr. Speaker, with a reference to something I read a long time ago. I will paraphrase it, but essentially it was to the effect that if you give a man or woman a fish, they will eat it and then it is gone. But if you help a man or woman to learn how to fish they will fish long afterwards. The theory of economic development is that they will then buy nets, hooks and cans from you. Then their economy will eventually hit what economists call the "take-off point", and they will soon join or surpass those of us who live in industrialized democracies.
At a United Nations Congress on crime prevention, of all things, a delegate from what we call the south part of the North-South dialogue said that the greatest crime he could think of was that the industrialized countries-he did not say Canada, but he might have-were out beating the Third World countries for what was, at the time, very scarce oil in the spot markets of the world. I remember feeling very guilty when he said that, because, as Hon. Members will know, Canada has subsidized the consumption of oil in this country in the last few years by about $17 billion. That seems to me- and I am sure it also seems to many other Members-to be an obscenely, unfair way of dealing with countries that have trouble feeding their people or providing oil for their people from the spot markets.
It has been said that Canada lives by trade that accounts for about 30 per cent of our gross national product. I would like to add some other reasons why I support Bill C-130, Mr. Speaker, and these relate to trade. It seems that the new trade policy, which we hope the Government will soon propose, will have a consensus in provincial governments, business, labour, and many other groups across the country. I think it should include the premises which follow.
First, Canada is dependent on international trade and there is the probability that that dependence will continue, if not
November 10, 1982

increase. 1 suggest that it will probably increase. Second, we should review the strong and weak sectors of our economy and identify foreign trade barriers that constrain the growth in the strong sectors. Third, Canada needs a negotiated and improved access on a multination trade basis, to export markets. Fourth, there is an additional need to negotiate reductions in foreign barriers that constrain the further processing in Canada of resource-based products prior to export. Fifth, the case is strong that the improvement and preservation of that access can best be done on a multilateral trading basis. Sixth, Canada's adjustment process to freer trade is a matter of importance for all levels of government in Canada.
I have with me a book, which I would commend to Flon. Members, entitled "Trade, Inflation, and the Dollar"-
[Translation}
-by Mr. Thibault de Saint Phalle, which was published in 1981 and which I find an excellent review of the present situation.
1 would like to summarize some of the points made by Mr. Thibault de Saint Phalle primarily in connection with the United States where he lives, and I would like to apply them to our own country in reference to this Bill. With respect to some of the agencies included in the Bill before us today, his book reads:
As it has turned out, the activities of the MDBs, have proved beneficial to both the poorer and richer nations. They are criticized, it sometimes seems, only because they have not found a way to help those who are not willing to help themselves. All in all, the creation of the MDBs must surely be considered one of the successful steps taken by the community of nations since the end of World War II to ensure that gradual economic development and an accompanying growth in trade could indeed be accomplished. The MDBs have performed their roles admirably, with few exceptions, ignoring politics in favour of economics and substituting active loan programs in place of empty rhetoric.
He went on to indicate that in his view the expansion of the MDBs, such as the ones about which we are talking today, are essential to the continued development of newly industrialized nations and to the continued expansion of world trade. It is hardly necessary to say that Canada is a prime player in world trade. I simply say, "Amen" to his comments.
To put it another way, the best way to help Canada find new markets for its products would be to encourage countries which have difficulties financing the purchases of products to buy them through credit facilities of institutions with which the Bill deals. I enthusiastically support the concept of these institutions, as should any Canadian interested in the longterm future of the country?
An important point, which cannot be made strongly enough, is that we should increase our exports-and which one of us in this room thinks that the Canadian economy is not strong enough to grow and thrive primarily by increasing our exports-to countries such as India, Indonesia, Brazil, Mexico, Philippines, Korea, Thailand, Colombia, Bangladesh, Yugoslavia-which perhaps is in a different category-Argentina, Morocco, Egypt, Turkey, Pakistan, Kenya, Peru, Malaysia
Financial Institutions
and the Dominican Republic, all of which are prime participants through these various regional development agencies in terms of financing exports from places such as our own country.
Many of the countries which I have just mentioned do not have the cash nor the necessary credit available to purchase Canadian products or the products of other industrialized countries without having an increased ability to finance them through institutions such as the ones included in the Bill. If we do not help these agencies to finance these countries, we will not have the free flow of commerce, which I believe the world very much needs. The expression "trade, not aid" has been used often, but it is more true today than ever before in world history that it is one of the ways the brotherhood of men and women will be realized on this planet.
It was suggested today in the House that these agencies are engaged in redistributing wealth from the so-called rich countries to the poor ones, to the detriment of working men and women in the former. Mr. de Saint Phalle dealt with that notion very well. I should say that this man has spent most of his life dealing with the matter of foreign trade. On the evidence available to him, he indicated that this view could not be supported and that these institutions were not taking advantage of the people in countries providing funds to them, and I agree with him.
One such institution is the InterAmerican Development Bank which was established in 1959 to aid Latin American nations in their development roles. It is true that American influence has been strong-and perhaps excessively strong-in that bank, but it is also true the bank has attempted to ensure that each country in Latin American obtained its share of the pie. Also I would like to say that IDB is directing more and more of its resources toward industrial and infrastructure products. Perhaps some part of the IDB might be merged in the future with the World Bank, but on balance it seems that the IDB has been a success. We are quite rightly proposing to increase our capital funding to the InterAmerican Development Bank.
The next institution to which I would like to refer is the Asian Development Bank. It has 41 members from Asia, Europe and North America. It was created to help Asian countries stabilize their domestic economies so that they might better resist external pressures and bring stability to their areas. Most of its loans are what they call hard loans to develop infrastructure. I think all of us should support that fully. It is a fact of life that Japan, being such a strong economy, would have the strong influence in that bank as it appears to have. That bank is working, and I submit that Canada should support it, as proposed in the Bill.
The third and last institution about which I would like to say a word or two is the African Development Fund which is a concessional lending Affiliate of the African Development Bank. It allows only African nations to be members, but the fund allows non-African countries to be members.
It is true the question can be raised as to whether we should have regional banks such as the ones mentioned in the Bill or

November 10, 1982
Financial Institutions
whether perhaps it would be better to have a less regional and more world conscious or world-oriented organization, but the reality of the matter is that these regional banks have grown up. It would seem to me that we should try to help them become more effective rather than make them less effective or even terminate some of them.
Since I have essentially said everything I hoped to say, perhaps it would be a very good time to end my remarks. But before doing so, I should like to mention that I feel as strongly as the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) in terms of the amendment we will be moving with respect to Clause 4 which would require Parliament to approve deletions or substitutions to the list of institutions named in the Bill rather than let the Governor in Council do it. I am sure that you will appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that it is Parliament not the Governor in Council that should be doing these things, especially when dealing with the expenditure of taxpayer's money. Apart from that caveat, I strongly urge other Members, both on this side of the House and on the other side, to approve the Bill in short order.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not take up too much time of the House this afternoon because I understand that when I complete my remarks we may be able to call it six o'clock and be able to head back to our ridings for a very important day tomorrow, it being Remembrance Day.
With respect to Bill C-130, basically what we are dealing with in this legislation are two age old conflicting arguments. They come into very sharp, clear focus at this particular time because of the economic situation in which we find ourselves in Canada. The age old argument which this Parliament has had to grapple with, and I would expect any democratic country in the world has had to grapple with, is whether or not, in our total Government spending, all our money in tough economic times should be spent right here in Canada or whether even in tough economic times part of our money, our Gross National Product, the money generated in the country, should be sent abroad to help those less fortunate than ourselves, those countries that we have targeted for assistance. That debate has gone on for a great length of time. It will continue for longer than many of us who are here today will be around.
How do we meet our double responsibility to this very serious problem? Economically, Canada is in trouble. We have heard other members talk about that this afternoon. We have people living on unemployment insurance benefits. We have people living on welfare. We have people who have problems
meeting payments at the end of the month. We have a serious problem with our native people in terms of straight, outright poverty. If Canada has a problem, can you imagine the kind of problem that some of the countries that are considered to be Third World countries have to deal with? That is the other side of the equation. When things are really tough in Canada, they are tough because we are not trading because of the world-wide recession, but they are tougher for other countries in the world.
How do we deal with this particular problem in these very difficult economic times? I support Bill C-130 and its intent. I am happy to say also that my party supports the whole intent of making sure that the international aid that we give to other countries will be maintained and the money will flow into other countries. We should support international development and we should support international aid. First and foremost what I consider to be the most important area is in the nongovernment organization sector.
As a Member of this House, together with some other Members of Parliament, I have spent the last 18 months carrying out a fairly detailed study into the whole question of Canada's relations with Latin America, the Caribbean and South America. It has been one of the most exhilarating experience 1 have had in the 12 years that I have been here as a Member of Parliament. This committee was largely nonpartisan. We tried to do a job that Canadians like to see us do, which was to take a non-partisan, objective approach in looking at the problem of Canada's relationship in the area of trade, aid and humanitarianism, in fact, in all of the facets in which Canada interacts with regions that are developing such as South America, Latin America and the Caribbean. We visited such countries as Haiti, Nicaragua, El Salvador, Brazil and Colombia. Canada contributes to international aid and development assistance in these countries. We do so in some cases to a fairly large extent. It is good to be able to stand in the House of Commons and say, for the most part, that that aid is being properly directed. It is reaching its goal, the people to whom it is intended to reach. Obviously it is not always the case, but for the most part it does.
This aid primarily is done through CIDA, our international agency. Canada gets a large measure of benefit from the kind of aid it gives. Canada is viewed as an objective country. In other words, Canada is a country that does not have any axe to grind with most of the countries with which we deal. Canada is viewed as being concerned with human rights. Part of that is attributed to the fact that we deal not in arms or military might or whether countries should do what we think they should do. We are perceived as a country that tries to do things for the good of the people in those countries. Our aid from that point of view is helpful.
In a number of cases the aid we give substantially helps the people to whom it is directed. But it is interesting to note that for the most part the aid that we give is best used when it has gone through non-government organization sectors. I am a firm believer that the best way Canada can provide aid to the
November 10, 1982

developing world is through self-help groups. If I were in charge, I would try to keep the money we spend away from governments at all levels, both ours and the countries with which we deal. I think that is important. If that can be achieved, then the greatest dollar value is gained within the particular country.
If we take a look at the number of people who are starving within the Third World, the most accurate figure or the most up-to-date figure that we have at the present time shows that at least 800 million people are suffering. This situation is getting worse, not better. These figures are rising.
I do not know how we as a Parliament or a country can turn our back on that kind of situation. From a humanitarian point of view alone, we have to participate. We are a country that trades on an international basis. The quid pro quo, if you like, is the fact that if we expect to trade with other countries, we then have to give something in return.
Some Hon. Members have indicated that we are spending too much money on international trade. Of course, I do not agree with that opinion. I think it is wrong. In fact, our total budget for CIDA is down some $245 million. Presently, Canada gives approximately 0.43 per cent of its GNP to our international trade. That is down, and it will probably be down from the long range objectives stated by the Government of approximately 0.5 per cent of our GNP by 1985. We will probably fall short of that objective. I believe that is a crime, which possibly says something about our country. The North-South task force, which, I believe, rightly spent a great deal of time looking into this question, is possibly one of the more authoritative works on the whole question of Canada's aid and trade. That task force discussed the target of approximately 0.75 per cent of our GNP by 1985. We will fall substantially short of that goal. The amount which we give falls short in comparison to what is given by United States and Japan for international aid.
We have a long way to go, Mr. Speaker. Whether we like it or not, there is a new era emerging. Hundreds of millions of people who are disadvantaged in the Third World want greater participation in what is happening in the world. We cannot turn the clock back to the 1950s or the 1960s. We must deal with the 1980s. If the reality that confronts us is the fact that more countries will not be satisfied with what they consider to be the status quo, we will have to change and enter into a more realistic era in the decade of the eighties. This means that while we may suffer problems in our own economic and social situation from time to time, brought on either by poor government policy or a world-wide recession in the developed countries, the flow of money going to the Third World will have to be maintained not only for humanitarian reasons but for self-interest reasons as well. It would be in our self interest to establish links with countries such as South America and Central America because our reputation would be enhanced and our trade made easier. This would make it more beneficial and profitable for all countries concerned.
Financial Institutions
Therefore, this question of aid is a very important one. At the present time we should be targeting our money toward self-help projects at the grassroots level, which help people directly, and agricultural oriented projects.
When our committee was in Colombia, we spent some time with an organization that I consider one of the better organizations that we have working in various parts of the world. It is the International Development Research Council. It is conducting agricultural based projects throughout the Third World, and certainly throughout Latin America. Canadians are benefiting from that work. Our reputation is being enhanced because Canadians are contributing to that area. That organization is spending its money wisely. As well, we are establishing that self-interest link which I have mentioned.
In conclusion, I would suggest that it would be a folly for us Canadians, regardless from what walk of life, to allow ourselves to become so narrow in our vision that even over the short term we will move toward reducing aid to the Third World. It may be argued that there is never a good time to spend money on a developing country. We could always find a sector of our country which is experiencing difficulties. We can always argue that we should not give further consideration to foreign aid until the next year. Of course this state of affairs would continue and that consideration would never take place.
I recently heard a report on the CBC news which indicated how desperately international aid is needed. It concerns approximately 200 Vietnamese who committed suicide. I wondered how this could happen in today's world. The reason they did this was that the children who were with this particular group in Vietnam would have starved. Therefore, they sacrificed themselves for the children. This same report indicated that there are about 8,000 people in this particular region who will starve to death in a very short time if agricultural and food aid is not sent to that area.
When I was preparing a few notes for this debate I was reflecting on the fact that incidents like these should not be allowed to happen in a world where, for example, North American countries have an abundance of agricultural products. In fact, we have so much that prices are depressed and farmers are in serious trouble. If these incidents do happen, we should strive with all our might and power never to let it happen again. That is the goal we should work toward. We can achieve it by developing a more realistic aid program which will meet, at least in part, the very desperate needs of the Third World.
